title: Refugees, returns and reconstruction: neighbouring states' perspectives on a new Syria
label: 3 November 2026 · Oral evidence
summary: Experts and the ambassadors of Lebanon and Türkiye told the Foreign Affairs Committee that many Syrians remain reluctant to return because basic services, security and livelihoods are not yet guaranteed; host countries have carried a heavy local burden and face strains as donor funds fall; camps in north‑east Syria collapsed chaotically, leaving some third‑country nationals unaccounted for; and the Committee heard practical suggestions for UK support focused on education, health, infrastructure and consular repatriation.

chapters.title: Why most Syrians are cautious about returning
chapters.takeaway: Many refugees want to return eventually, but they need security, schools, housing and jobs first—'dignified' return is the repeated requirement.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To start: how has the refugee situation changed since Assad fell?

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Syria lost about half its population during the war—roughly 6 million fled abroad, 6 million were displaced internally. After 2024 some elites returned, but the majority remain cautious.

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: People want to return with dignity and safety. Schools, health clinics, hospitals and neighbourhoods were destroyed; many feel those basics aren’t ready yet.

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Return isn't uniform. Some people have created lives in host countries—young people who grew up abroad may not want to or be able to go back immediately.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What drives the returns we have seen?

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Those who could access housing and work tended to go back; many on the fence lack those basics and prefer the predictability, however limited, of life in the host country.

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Women especially cite safety and freedom concerns. Parents will not return until they can be confident about schools and security for their daughters.

chapters.title: Host countries: strains, responses and donor fatigue
chapters.takeaway: Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan bore heavy, different burdens; donor aid was often short‑term and has fallen, leaving local systems strained.

turns.speaker: Abtisam Mohamed
turns.text: How have neighbouring countries coped economically and socially with refugees?

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Turkey adopted temporary protection and gave access to healthcare and education, even citizenship to some; overall economic effects were mixed and some sectors grew.

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Macro studies show limited national impact, but local communities and services have been overwhelmed, creating tensions and insecurity.

turns.speaker: Haneen Sayed
turns.text: Lebanon hosted the largest number per capita—around 1.5 million refugees on a 4 million population—straining schools, hospitals, water and electricity and depressing wages.

turns.speaker: Haneen Sayed
turns.text: We worked with the UN and donors, ran afternoon school shifts and health programmes, but donor funding has fallen and the public system remains weak.

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Aid often came as short-term humanitarian funding, creating parallel services and NGO dependency rather than strengthening national systems.

turns.speaker: Jessica Toale
turns.text: Could donors organise aid better?

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Yes. More long‑term investment in health and education systems—so host communities and refugees benefit—would be more effective than short cycles of humanitarian aid.

chapters.title: Education, skills and a 'lost generation'
chapters.takeaway: Many refugee children missed school or only got reduced 'second shift' classes; without fixing education, returning Syrians cannot rebuild the country.

turns.speaker: Alex Ballinger
turns.text: What about the education refugees received—can it support return or local integration?

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Turkey did better on gradual integration into national schools. Lebanon used second‑shift schooling; about 40% of Syrian children in Lebanon attend school and many don't reach secondary level.

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: That creates a risk of a lost generation and deskilled teachers—Syrian teachers couldn't work legally in Lebanon or Jordan, so their skills eroded.

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Education reform in Syria will be decisive for returns. There's debate about the curriculum; if it becomes more conservative and restricts women's representation, that will deter parents.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the UK could help with curricula and rebuilding schools?

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Exactly. The UK should focus on supporting education and health systems—not just emergency aid—so people feel a dignified path to return.

chapters.title: The camps and unaccounted third‑country nationals
chapters.takeaway: The collapse of al‑Hawl was chaotic; many were displaced, thousands went to prisons in Iraq, and dozens of third‑country nationals—mainly women and children—remain unaccounted for or detained.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Harmonie, tell us what happened in the north‑east camps and why we should worry about British citizens there.

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: In early 2026 al‑Hawl collapsed in chaos after fighting; prisoners from several facilities—about 5,700 men and boys—were transferred to prisons in Iraq by US or US‑backed forces.

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: Al‑Roj still holds mostly women and children—several thousand people in total—and we estimate just over 40 British nationals remain, mostly children.

turns.speaker: Edward Morello
turns.text: Have there been repatriations?

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: Very few. The last UK repatriation I know was in April 2025—one woman and three children. Other countries—France, the Netherlands, Australia, Norway, Finland and the US—have repatriated more citizens.

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: The UK's stated obstacles—no consular presence in Syria—are less persuasive given continued contact with Syrian authorities and an embassy in Iraq; many children are recognised as British and vulnerable.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is it feasible for the UK to repatriate those children?

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: Yes. The UK has strong counter‑terror systems and can manage reintegration. Leaving children in harsh camp conditions—or asking them to be separated from mothers—raises serious protection concerns.

chapters.title: Opportunities and geopolitical challenges for reconstruction
chapters.takeaway: Türkiye sees economic opportunities in a stable Syria and is investing in jobs and industrial zones; Lebanon seeks help to make returns sustainable and to rebuild services.

turns.speaker: Osman Koray Ertaş
turns.text: Türkiye hosted 3.7 million Syrians at peak and still protects about 2.2 million; since 2024 more than 770,000 have voluntarily returned.

turns.speaker: Osman Koray Ertaş
turns.text: We want Syria to be stable and investable. We're planning industrial zones in Aleppo and Damascus, reconnecting trade and infrastructure, and aiming to create jobs to make returns sustainable.

turns.speaker: Edward Morello
turns.text: Will Turkey keep troops in northern Syria?

turns.speaker: Osman Koray Ertaş
turns.text: Our presence has been with Syrian consent and is shifting towards training and transferring civilian services to Syrian authorities; final decisions will depend on security improvements.

turns.speaker: Farah Berry
turns.text: Lebanon thanks the UK for past support. We ask continued help financing schools, hospitals and housing so returns are not just crossings but sustainable lives in dignity.

turns.speaker: Haneen Sayed
turns.text: We set out a return plan with IOM/UNHCR support: modest cash assistance to families and removing penalties for overstaying, which has led to 650–700,000 returns from Lebanon since it began.

turns.speaker: Haneen Sayed
turns.text: Some refugees will want to stay where they built lives; Lebanon cannot naturalise large numbers, but we can legalise work and residency where appropriate.

chapters.title: Practical steps the UK and partners could take
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses urged the UK to prioritise rebuilding education and health systems, support infrastructure and financial channels, and actively pursue consular repatriation for vulnerable nationals.

turns.speaker: Jessica Toale
turns.text: Concretely, what should the UK do differently?

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Shift funding from short humanitarian cycles to longer‑term support for public education and health so host countries and refugees benefit and returns become realistic.

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Donors should avoid creating parallel systems; invest in national schools and hospitals and in training Syrian teachers and medical staff so skills are preserved for reconstruction.

turns.speaker: Osman Koray Ertaş
turns.text: The UK can cooperate on financial services, infrastructure projects and project‑based support. TİKA and FCDO are already in discussion on specific projects.

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: On the camp issue, the UK should actively track and repatriate British children and vulnerable nationals; many other countries have succeeded and the UK has the capabilities.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final disagreements or cautions?

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Be cautious about blanket security advice: parts of Damascus and Aleppo are relatively safe now; a nuanced approach helps researchers and practitioners understand the real situation on the ground.

turns.speaker: Haneen Sayed
turns.text: Finally: helping Syria rebuild is also in Lebanon’s and the region’s interest—stability there reduces pressure on neighbouring states and creates economic opportunities for all.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. Please send any further evidence in writing.
